analysis.one_liner: Bans class-action lawsuits alleging companies misclassified employees as independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have blocked gig-economy workers from banding together in class actions over misclassification, never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the rules for federal class-action lawsuits so that no class action could proceed if the claim is that workers were wrongly labeled independent contractors instead of employees. Gig-economy companies like ride-share and delivery platforms rely heavily on classifying workers as contractors, which avoids paying payroll taxes, benefits, and overtime. Misclassification lawsuits are the main way those workers can challenge the label as a group; this bill would take that tool away, while leaving each worker to sue alone, which few can afford.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that use large numbers of independent contractors — especially gig platforms like ride-share and delivery apps — would be shielded from class-wide lawsuits over misclassification. That means lower exposure to back-pay, tax, and benefit claims from workers. Even a company sued by an individual worker could not face the far larger class action behind it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig platforms and heavy users of contractors

how_it_helps.text: Amends Rule 23 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure to add a new requirement for class certification: the claim must not allege misclassification of employees as independent contractors [S2][S3].
States its purpose as protecting the 'gig economy' and small businesses that operate largely through contractor services from 'costly class action litigation' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who believe they were wrongly denied employee status — and the overtime, benefits, and payroll taxes that come with it — would lose the class action, the one affordable way to challenge the label collectively. Individual lawsuits are expensive and risky, so most misclassified workers would be left with no practical remedy.

drawbacks.text: A worker who was misclassified could still sue individually, but as a practical matter few can carry the cost and risk of a solo federal lawsuit against a large platform, so the remedy would mostly exist on paper [S2][S3].

Because the amendment is written into the general class-certification rule, it would bar misclassification class actions against any employer, not just gig platforms — including larger businesses that misclassify workers, not only the small businesses the bill's title emphasizes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers litigation-cost relief to contractor-dependent businesses, which is a real interest, but it buys that relief by eliminating the primary legal tool misclassified workers have. The loss falls on people with little bargaining power; the gain goes to companies that save on wages, benefits, and payroll taxes by using contractor labels. Weighed honestly, the costs to workers outweigh the protections for businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Introduced March 21, 2018 by Rep. Andy Biggs (R-AZ) [S1][S2].
Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction; it received no cosponsors [S4][S5].
Referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice on April 30, 2018, where it remained with no further action through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig-economy companies and other employers that rely on independent contractor labels keep facing the same legal exposure they already had — which for them means no change, and for misclassified workers means their class-action rights were never taken away. The bill's sponsor and contractor-dependent businesses are the ones spared a lost fight; workers lose nothing because nothing passed.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Bob Goodlatte)
against.role: Committee of referral; no markup was ever scheduled
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on April 30, 2018 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so its support never took a partisan shape beyond its lone Republican sponsor [S4][S5].

industries.note: These companies build their business model on classifying workers as independent contractors, avoiding benefits, payroll taxes, and overtime. The bill would have removed their biggest legal risk — a class action over that classification — leaving each worker to sue alone. The bill died, so the gain never materialized.

Any business that relies heavily on contractors would have gained protection from misclassification class actions, at the direct expense of workers trying to challenge the label. The bill died, so nothing changed.
The bill would have wiped out the misclassification class action, a core tool for representing groups of misclassified workers affordably. It died, so the tool remains available.
